title: Content Plan, Social Media Graphics and Copy
unit: Create content · LO1 Plan and LO2 Produce digital marketing content

lesson.html:
Day 2 is face-to-face in the computer laboratory. By the end of the day you should be able to:

  1. communicate the purpose, goals and vision of content for an MSME;
  2. identify the audience and select platforms, equipment and tools;
  3. research content keywords and build a two-week content calendar; and
  4. produce social media graphics with legal media and proofread persuasive copy.

The activities follow Task Sheet 1.1-1 (content plan and calendar) and Task Sheet 2.1-1 (graphics and copy). You work in the lab's Content Planner and Post Composer; design the graphics in Canva, then upload them to the composer.

lesson.h: Part 2 — Purpose, Audience, Platforms and Tools
lesson.html:
Information Sheet 1.1-1

After this part you should be able to:

  1. explain basic marketing principles and the purpose, goals and vision of a brand;
  2. describe the digital marketing channels and platforms;
  3. identify the audience (cold, warm, hot, active customers) based on messaging; and
  4. select platforms, equipment and tools based on the identified audience.

Digital Marketing

Digital marketing is the promotion of brands, products and services to potential customers using the internet and other digital communication. Digital marketing content is anything a brand publishes to attract, engage and convert its audience: posts, graphics, videos, blog articles, e-mails and ads.

Basic Marketing Principles: the 4 Ps

PQuestionExample: Kape't Alon Cafe, San Juan, La Union
ProductWhat do we sell and what problem does it solve?Iced coffee and pandesal for surfers and tourists
PriceHow much, and how does it compare?P149 breakfast set; weekend promo 10% off
PlaceWhere can customers buy?Beachfront shop; orders through Facebook Messenger
PromotionHow do customers learn about it?Instagram Reels, TikTok videos, Facebook posts, Google Maps listing

Purpose, Goals and Vision

Every piece of content must support what the business wants to achieve. Communicate these three statements before you create anything:

StatementAnswersExample
VisionWhat the brand wants to become in the long term"The favorite coffee stop of every surfer in La Union"
PurposeWhy the content existsMake more people aware of the cafe and its breakfast set
Goals (SMART)Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound targets"Reach 15,000 people and get 60 Messenger orders in 2 weeks"

Digital Marketing Channels

ChannelBest forContent formats
Social mediaAwareness, engagement, communityPosts, carousels, Reels/TikTok, stories, live video
BlogSearch traffic, trust, detailed informationArticles, guides, reviews
VlogStorytelling and demonstrationsYouTube videos, Shorts
E-mailRepeat customers, offers, newslettersNewsletters, promos, reminders
AdsFast, targeted reachBoosted posts, image/video ads, search ads

Audience and Messaging

The same message does not work for everyone. Identify the audience temperature and match the message:

AudienceWho they areMessage that worksExample content
ColdNever heard of the brandAttention and value: entertain or teachReel: "3 surf spots near San Juan + where to get coffee"
WarmKnow the brand, have interactedProof and reasons to choose youCustomer reviews, behind-the-scenes, menu carousel
HotReady to buy, showed intentOffer and clear call to action"Weekend promo: 10% off - message us to reserve"
Active customersAlready boughtLoyalty and referralLoyalty card post, "tag a friend" promo

Selecting Platforms

Choose platforms where the identified audience already spends time, and that fit the content you can produce:

PlatformMain audience in the PhilippinesStrength
FacebookBroadest, all ages; local communities and groupsPosts, events, Messenger orders, Marketplace
InstagramYoung adults, travel and lifestyleVisual feed, Reels, stories
TikTokTeens to young adults, fast-growing for all agesShort video discovery, trends
YouTubeAll ages, search-drivenLong and short video, tutorials, reviews
LinkedInProfessionals, business-to-businessThought leadership, hiring, B2B services
Blog / websitePeople searching on GoogleSearch traffic, credibility, detailed content

Digital Marketing Equipment and Tools

TypeExamplesUse
EquipmentLaptop or desktop, smartphone or camera, tripod, LED light, condenser or lavalier microphone, headphones with microphoneCapture and edit photos, videos and audio
Design toolsCanva, Adobe Express, PhotopeaGraphics, carousels, thumbnails
Video and photo editing toolsCapCut, DaVinci Resolve, SnapseedCut, caption, color and export videos
Word processing toolsGoogle Docs, Microsoft WordCopy, scripts, blog drafts
Scheduling toolsMeta Business Suite, TikTok scheduler, YouTube StudioPlan and auto-publish content
Time-tracking toolsToggl, ClockifyTrack production time per client
Remember: Select equipment and tools based on the audience. A TikTok audience expects vertical, fast, phone-shot video; a LinkedIn audience expects clean graphics and well-written posts.

lesson.h: Part 3 — Keyword Research and the Content Calendar
lesson.html:
Information Sheet 1.1-2

After this part you should be able to:

  1. research content keywords according to the purpose of the content;
  2. use free keyword and trend tools;
  3. formulate a digital marketing content calendar according to its purpose and goals; and
  4. use scheduling tools and apply data and analytics in planning.

Content Keywords

A content keyword is a word or phrase that describes what a piece of content is about and that the audience types when searching. Keywords are used in blog titles, captions, video titles and hashtags so that search engines and platform algorithms show the content to the right people.

Keyword typeExampleUse
Short-tail"coffee"Very competitive; too broad for a small business
Long-tail"iced coffee near San Juan La Union"Fewer searches but ready-to-buy audience - best for MSMEs
Local"cafe in Laoag City"Local SEO and Google Maps
Hashtag#SanJuanLaUnion, #SurfCafeDiscovery on Instagram and TikTok

Free Keyword Research Tools

  1. Google search suggestions - type the topic and note the autocomplete phrases and "People also ask" questions.
  2. Google Trends - compare the popularity of terms over time and by region (e.g., "surfing" in La Union vs Ilocos Norte).
  3. Google Keyword Planner (free with a Google Ads account) - search volume ranges and related keywords.
  4. Platform search bars - TikTok, YouTube and Instagram search suggestions and trending hashtags.
  5. Competitor content - note the words competitors use in top-performing posts.

Record the results in a keyword list: keyword, type, purpose (awareness, consideration, sales) and where it will be used.

The Content Calendar

A content calendar is the plan of what will be published, when, on which platform, and why. It keeps posting consistent, connects every post to a goal, and lets the client approve the content before production.

  • Columns: date, platform, content type, topic or hook, keyword or hashtag, call to action, status (draft, approved, scheduled, published).
  • Mix content: about 70% value (educational, entertaining), 20% engagement (questions, user content), 10% direct offers.
  • Include local events and seasons: summer surf season, fiestas, holidays, payday weekends.
  • Plan a realistic frequency for the resources of the MSME (e.g., 4-5 posts per week).

Content calendars are usually kept in a spreadsheet or a project tool. The example below is written in HTML so you can see the structure; the screenshot shows how it looks in a browser.

Scheduling Tools

  • Meta Business Suite - schedule Facebook and Instagram posts, Reels and stories; view insights.
  • TikTok - schedule videos on the web version (TikTok Studio).
  • YouTube Studio - schedule uploads and premieres.
  • Schedule at the times the audience is active; check the platform insights ("when your followers are online").

Data and Analytics in Planning

Use last month's insights to plan: which content types had the highest engagement, which days and times worked, and which topics brought messages or orders. Plan more of what worked and test one new idea each week.

Law: Online sellers must follow the E-Commerce Act of 2000 (RA 8792): electronic documents and transactions are valid, and misleading online offers can be penalized. Plan promos with clear terms (dates, conditions).

lesson.h: Part 4 — Visual Design for Social Media Graphics
lesson.html:
Information Sheet 2.1-1

After this part you should be able to:

  1. apply the elements and principles of visual design;
  2. create social media graphics and featured images in the correct sizes;
  3. add media to draft content in accordance with the content plan and copyright law.

Elements of Visual Design

ElementMeaningTip for social media
ColorHue, value and saturation; brand colorsUse 2-3 brand colors; keep strong contrast between text and background
TypographyFonts, sizes and weightsUse at most 2 fonts; headline large and bold, body simple
ImagePhotos, illustrations, iconsOne clear subject; good light; no stretched or blurry images
Shape and lineBoxes, circles, dividersGroup related information; guide the eye to the call to action
SpaceEmpty area around elementsWhite (negative) space makes the message readable

Principles of Design

PrincipleWhat it does
HierarchyThe most important information (offer, headline) is seen first; details come after
ContrastDifferences in color, size and weight make key elements stand out
AlignmentElements line up to a grid, giving a clean, professional look
BalanceVisual weight is distributed evenly (symmetrical or asymmetrical)
Repetition / consistencyThe same colors, fonts and logo placement build brand recognition
ProximityRelated items are placed together (price next to product)

Compare two graphics for the same promo. Both are built with HTML and CSS so you can study how the design decisions are made; the screenshots show the result.

Common Sizes

ContentSize (pixels)Aspect ratio
Feed post (Facebook, Instagram)1080 x 1080 or 1080 x 13501:1 or 4:5
Story, Reel, TikTok, YouTube Shorts1080 x 19209:16
YouTube thumbnail / blog featured image1280 x 72016:9
Facebook cover (page)1640 x 624 (safe area in the center)about 2.6:1

Adding Media Legally

  • Use your own photos and videos, or media licensed for commercial use (e.g., Canva Pro content, royalty-free libraries such as Pexels and Pixabay - read each license).
  • Never copy images from Google search or other pages without permission: this violates the Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293) as amended by RA 10372.
  • Get written consent before posting identifiable customers or staff (Data Privacy Act of 2012, RA 10173).
  • Keep a media log: file name, source, license, date - it proves the content is legal.

lesson.h: Part 5 — Copywriting, Brand Voice and Proofreading
lesson.html:
Information Sheet 2.1-2

After this part you should be able to:

  1. write persuasive copy using copywriting frameworks, brand voice and storytelling;
  2. proofread copy according to the buyer's requirements; and
  3. apply pertinent laws, platform policies and codes of conduct to digital marketing content.

Copywriting Frameworks

FrameworkStepsExample caption
AIDAAttention - Interest - Desire - Action"Tired after your dawn surf? (A) Our iced latte is brewed from Benguet beans (I). Pair it with warm pandesal for only P149 (D). Message us to reserve your set! (A)"
PASProblem - Agitate - Solution"No time for breakfast before class? Skipping it makes you tired by 10 AM. Grab our 5-minute breakfast set on the way."
Before-After-BridgeSituation now - better situation - how to get there"Before: warm canned coffee. After: a cold, creamy latte by the sea. The bridge: Kape't Alon, 50 steps from the beach."

Brand Voice and Storytelling

  • Brand voice is the consistent personality of the brand's words: e.g., friendly, local and energetic ("Tara, kape tayo!"). Write it down in 3 adjectives with "do" and "don't" examples.
  • Storytelling: a character (customer), a problem, and how the product helps. Real stories of local customers build trust.
  • Write for the platform: short and punchy on TikTok and Instagram; more detail on Facebook and the blog.

Proofreading Checklist

The CS lists what must be checked before content is approved:

CheckQuestion to ask
KeywordsAre the planned keywords and hashtags used naturally?
Grammar and spellingIs the English/Filipino correct? Are names and prices spelled right?
StructureDoes the copy start with a hook and end with one clear call to action?
Tone and brand voiceDoes it sound like the brand?
ComplianceDoes it follow laws, platform rules and ad restrictions? Are promo terms clear?
Trigger wordsAre there words that platforms flag or that offend (e.g., exaggerated health claims, "guaranteed income")?
Relevance and accuracyIs every fact, price, date and claim true and current?

Pertinent Policies, Regulations and Laws

Law / policyWhat it means for content creators
RA 8293 Intellectual Property Code, as amended by RA 10372Do not use others' music, images, videos or text without a license; respect trademarks
RA 8792 E-Commerce Act of 2000Online transactions and documents are valid; online offers must be honest
RA 10173 Data Privacy Act of 2012Get consent before collecting or posting personal information; protect customer data
RA 10175 Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012Online libel, identity theft and illegal access are crimes - no false accusations or fake reviews
Anti-piracy rulesNo pirated software, fonts, music or movies in content production
Platform community standardsEach platform bans certain content (hate, violence, misleading health claims); violations remove posts or pages

activities.title: Content Strategy for an MSME
activities.html:
Task Sheet 1.1-1, steps 1 to 4. Open the Content Planner and fill in each card for your MSME (see Lesson Part 6 if you need a practice client).

  1. Interview the MSME owner (or read the client brief): products, prices, customers, current pages and goals.
  2. Write the vision, purpose and two SMART goals of the content.
  3. Describe the audience in three temperatures (cold, warm, hot) with one key message each.
  4. Select two or three platforms and justify each with the audience; list the equipment and tools you will use.

The checklist under Answers turns green as you complete each card. Your trainer, acting as the client, grades the quality with the Performance Criteria Checklist.

activities.title: Keyword Research and Two-Week Content Calendar
activities.html:
Task Sheet 1.1-1, steps 5 to 8. In the Content Planner, research the keywords, then plan the calendar. Your goals and platforms from Activity 2.1 are shown at the top.

  1. Research at least 10 keywords and hashtags (long-tail and local) using Google search, Google Trends and platform search.
  2. Build a two-week content calendar (at least 8 posts) with date, platform, type, hook, keyword, call to action and status.
  3. Check the content mix (value, engagement, offers) and the promo terms (RA 8792).
  4. Present the plan to the trainer (acting as the client) for approval; revise if needed.

The format of a content calendar:

parts.prompt: Keyword list and content calendar (Content Planner)

checks.label: 10 or more keywords, each with a type and a purpose
At least 4 long-tail or local keywords
At least 2 hashtags
8 or more complete posts (date, platform, type, hook, keyword, CTA, mix)
Posts on two or more platforms
At least half of the posts give value (teach / entertain)
Offers are 30% of the posts or fewer
Every post has a status

parts.prompt: Quality of the keywords and calendar, and the presentation to the client (trainer)
criteria: Did you research content keywords according to the purpose?
Did you formulate a content calendar according to the purpose and goals?
Did you present the plan to the client (trainer) and revise it as asked?

activities.title: Social Media Graphics and Proofread Copy
activities.html:
Task Sheet 2.1-1. Design the three graphics in Canva (Create a design › Custom size), download them as PNG or JPG, then upload each one to its slot in the Post Composer. The preview shows how the post will look on the platform.

  1. Photograph the product with your smartphone or the DSLR camera, LED light and backdrop (at least 5 photos); record them in the media log.
  2. Design three graphics following the content calendar: a 1080 x 1080 feed post, a 1080 x 1350 promo and a 1080 x 1920 story.
  3. Apply hierarchy, contrast, alignment and brand consistency; add the logo and one clear call to action.
  4. Write the caption of each graphic using AIDA or PAS in the brand voice; add 3-5 hashtags.
  5. Proofread each caption with the checklist of Information Sheet 2.1-2 and fix all issues.
  6. Check the media log: every image is your own or licensed; consent obtained for identifiable persons.
  7. Export the graphics (PNG/JPG) and save them with the captions in your portfolio folder.

Compare a poor and a good graphic (Lesson Part 4):

checks.label: Post 1 graphic is 1080 × 1080 (1:1)
Post 2 graphic is 1080 × 1350 (4:5)
Post 3 graphic is 1080 × 1920 (9:16)
Every post has a platform
Every caption has 80 to 2,200 characters
Every caption has 3 to 5 hashtags
Every post has one call to action
Every caption proofread (all 7 checks)
Media log: 3 or more files with source, license and consent
No media with missing consent

parts.prompt: Quality of the graphics and copy (trainer)
criteria: Did you create the graphics according to the purpose and goals of the content plan?
Did you add media as planned, using only own or licensed images with consent where needed?
Did you apply the elements and principles of design and brand consistency?
Did you write persuasive copy using a copywriting framework and the brand voice?
Did you proofread the copy for keywords, grammar, tone, compliance and accuracy?
Did you follow the pertinent laws and platform policies?
